label: UV-C light
summary: UV-C germicidal lamps in water and air purifiers, air-conditioning ducts and sterilising cabinets burn the eyes and skin within seconds to minutes. Eye pain usually starts hours later, so you don't know you were hurt until it's done. Some lamps also make ozone, and fluorescent-type UV lamps contain mercury.
signs: Clear quartz tubes or bulbs, not frosted or white-coated, labelled UV-C, UVC or germicidal
Lamps inside water purifier chambers, air purifiers, ductwork and sterilising cabinets
A faint blue-violet glow from a clear tube
A sharp, clean smell like after a thunderstorm: ozone
Warning labels about eye and skin exposure
do: Run UV-C lamps only inside a closed housing
Fit or keep a switch that turns the lamp off when the housing is opened
Check it's lit through a small window of ordinary glass or clear polycarbonate, which block UV-C
Handle lamps by the ends, and treat a broken one like a mercury spill
dont: Don't look at a bare lit UV-C lamp, even for a moment
Don't expose your skin to it
Don't use it to disinfect people, pets, or rooms with people in them
Don't run ozone-making lamps where people sleep
ppe: UV-rated eye protection (a UV mark on the lens, or EN 166), or a face shield over safety glasses; a visor with no rating may not block enough
firstAid: Gritty, painful, watering eyes 6–12 hours after exposure: rest in a dark room with eyes closed and a cool damp cloth on them
It usually heals in 1–2 days; if it doesn't, or vision stays blurred, get medical care
Skin: treat like sunburn; cool it, shade it and keep it covered
